{{Short description|Theorem in number theory}}
{{for|Lagrange's other theorems|Lagrange's theorem (disambiguation)}}
In [[number theory]], '''Lagrange's theorem''' is a statement named after [[Joseph-Louis Lagrange]] about how frequently a [[polynomial]] over the [[integer]]s may evaluate to a multiple of a fixed [[Prime number|prime]] ''p''. More precisely, it states that for all integer polynomials <math>\textstyle f \in \mathbb{Z}[x]</math>, either:
* every coefficient of {{math|''f''}} is divisible by ''p'', or
* <math> p \mid f(x) </math> has at most {{math|deg ''f''}} solutions in {{math|{{mset|1, 2, ..., ''p''}}}},

where {{math|deg ''f''}} is the [[Degree of a polynomial|degree]] of {{math|''f''}}.

This can be stated with [[Modular arithmetic|congruence classes]] as follows: for all polynomials <math>\textstyle f \in (\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})[x]</math> with ''p'' prime, either:
* every coefficient of {{math|''f''}} is null, or
* <math> f(x)=0 </math> has at most {{math|deg ''f''}} solutions in <math> \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z} </math>.

If ''p'' is not prime, then there can potentially be more than {{math|deg ''f''(''x'')}} solutions. Consider for example ''p=8'' and the polynomial ''f(x)=x''{{i sup|''2''}}''−1'', where ''1, 3, 5, 7'' are all solutions.

==Proof==

Let <math>\textstyle f \in \mathbb{Z}[x]</math> be an integer polynomial, and write {{math|''g'' &isin; ('''Z'''/''p'''''Z''')[''x'']}} the polynomial obtained by taking its coefficients {{math|mod ''p''}}. Then, for all integers ''x'',

<math> f(x) \equiv 0 \pmod{p} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad g(x) \equiv 0 \pmod{p} </math>.

Furthermore, by the [[Modular_arithmetic#Basic_properties|basic rules]] of modular arithmetic,

<math> f(x) \equiv 0 \pmod{p} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(x \bmod{p}) \equiv 0 \pmod{p} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad g(x \bmod{p}) \equiv 0 \pmod{p} </math>.

Both versions of the theorem (over {{math|'''Z'''}} and over {{math|'''Z'''/''p'''''Z'''}}) are thus equivalent. We prove the second version by induction on the degree, in the case where the coefficients of ''f'' are not all null.

If {{math|deg ''f'' {{=}} 0}} then {{mvar|f}} has no roots and the statement is true.

If {{math|deg ''f'' ≥ 1}} without roots then the statement is also trivially true.

Otherwise, {{math|deg ''f'' ≥ 1}} and {{mvar|f}} has a root <math> k\in\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z} </math>.
The fact that {{math|'''Z'''/''p'''''Z'''}} is a field allows to apply the [[Polynomial long division|division algorithm]] to {{mvar|f}} and the polynomial {{math|''x'' &minus; ''k''}} (of degree ''1''), which yields the existence of a polynomial <math>\textstyle g \in (\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})[x]</math> (of degree lower than that of {{mvar|f}}) and of a constant <math>\textstyle r \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}</math> (of degree lower than ''1'') such that

<math> f(x) = g(x) (x-k) + r.</math>

Evaluating at {{math|''x'' {{=}} ''k''}} provides {{math|''r'' {{=}} 0}}.<ref>[[Factor theorem#Proof_3]]</ref> The other roots of ''f'' are then roots of ''g'' as well, which by the induction property are at most {{math|deg ''g'' ≤ deg ''f'' &minus; 1}} in number. This proves the result.

==Generalization==

Let {{math|''p''(''X'')}} be a polynomial over an [[integral domain]] {{mvar|R}} with degree {{math|''n'' > 0}}.
Then the polynomial equation {{math|1=''p''(''x'') = 0}} has at most {{math|1=''n'' = deg(''p''(''X''))}} roots in {{mvar|R}}.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://web.mat.bham.ac.uk/R.W.Kaye/teaching/modules/msm203a/chapter3.pdf#page=2|title=Polynomials and rings Chapter 3: Integral domains and fields}} Theorem 1.7.</ref>
